method: All printed pages read from the supplied PDFs at 2x-3x zoom (whole-page renders plus glyph-level checks of every number and ambiguous token), with explicit local traversals recorded per page. Ordered source blocks include every instructional bullet, table row/cell, flowchart step, diagram label, arrow annotation, legend entry and caption. Contiguous labels share an item when needed; consolidation items sit after the lines they test and never pull later material forward. Headers, timestamps, footers and blank Active space excluded.
caveats: Ch8 p748-752: auto-generated source checklist from existing 83 questions, each mapped to its printed line in book order. Visual scan was read at 3x zoom; any printed unit errors or ambiguous glyphs are taught as printed and flagged in explanations where known. No new medical facts introduced beyond the scan.

elements.source: The initial investigation of kidney disease pairs USG abdomen and renal function tests with: [Initial investigation: ultrasonography (USG) abdomen, renal function test (RFT) and urine analysis. (Book p748)]
For protein estimation in the initial urine analysis, the preferred test is: [Urine analysis: 24hr protein (preferred), albumin/creatinine, protein/creatinine. (Book p748)]
The RFT arm of the initial investigation measures: [RFT: S. urea, S. creatinine, S. Na+, S. K+. (Book p748)]
On the USG approach, a kidney size below which value points toward chronic kidney disease? [Look for: kidney size <8 cm. (Book p748)]
Kidneys larger than 10 cm with loss of corticomedullary differentiation are classically seen with: [>10 cm with loss of CMD with: DM, HIV, amyloidosis. (Book p748)]

Enlarged (>10 cm) kidneys with loss of CMD are listed for all of the following EXCEPT: [Loss of CMD with >10 cm kidneys: DM, HIV, amyloidosis; vesicoureteral reflux belongs to the asymmetric-kidney note. (Book p748)]
Fill up: On the USG approach, seeing corticomedullary differentiation (CMD) places the patient in the ______ arm. [CMD present → CKD; absent → non-CKD. (Book p748)]

Match each normal-kidney USG structure with its echogenicity — 1) Cortex 2) Pyramids 3) Fat, calyx, sinus, vessels … A) Hyperechoic B) Isoechoic C) Hypoechoic [Isoechoic: cortex; hypoechoic: pyramids; hyperechoic: fat, calyx, sinus, vessels. (Book p748)]
Which statement about the USG approach is TRUE? [USG abdomen (most important); CMD present → CKD, absent → non-CKD; 8-10 cm loss of CMD is itself a CKD clue. (Book p748)]
The two end-point branches drawn for established CKD are: [CKD → hemodialysis / transplant. (Book p748)]

Under 'Urine Analysis' in the initial-investigation flowchart, the box marked (Preferred) sits beside which two boxes? [Urine analysis branches into three printed boxes: 24hr Protein (Preferred), Albumin/Creatinine and Protein/Creatinine — i.e. the ratio tests that supp]

The normal-kidney ultrasound figure lists several hyperechoic structures; which of these is NOT in that list? [The labels read Isoechoic: Cortex; Hypoechoic: Pyramid; Hyperechoic: Fat, Calyx, sinus, vessels — the pyramid is the hypoechoic structure. (Book p748)]

The pair of ultrasound images drawn under 'Chronic Kidney Failure' is captioned 'Cortico medullary differentiation (CMD) lost'. [The USG ABDOMEN – In CKD diagram contrasts a normal kidney (with cortex/pyramid labels) against chronic kidney failure images captioned 'Cortico medul]

Fill up: In the 'Look for' list, kidneys measuring 8–10 cm are described by the finding of ______ of CMD. [The three printed size lines are: kidney size <8 cm; 8–10 cm loss of CMD; >10 cm with loss of CMD with DM, HIV, amyloidosis. (Book p748)]

A 46-year-old with raised creatinine has bilaterally 7.4 cm kidneys on ultrasound. According to the 'Look for' list, this size band: [The first bullet of the look-for list is 'Kidney size <8 cm', which the flowchart uses to place the patient under chronic kidney disease. (Book p748)]

In the approach flowchart, corticomedullary differentiation marked 'Absent' leads to which label? [As printed, CMD 'Present' runs down to Chronic kidney disease (CKD) and then to Hemodialysis or Transplant, while 'Absent' is routed to Non-CKD — the ]

elements.source: Before diagnosing CKD on USG one must rule out hydronephroureteronephrosis, whose clue on imaging is: [Rule out hydronephroureteronephrosis before diagnosing CKD; calyces becoming prominent and ureter seen. (Book p749)]

Match each tempo with its non-CKD category — 1) Hours to days 2) Days to weeks 3) Normal RFT with renal disease … A) Acute kidney injury (AKI) B) Rapidly progressive renal failure (RPRF) C) Nephrotic syn / RTA type I-II / asymptomatic urine abnormality [Hours to days → AKI; days to weeks → RPRF; normal RFT with renal disease → nephrotic syn, RTA I/II, asymptomatic urine abnormality. (Book p749)]
The AKI arm of the flowchart lists postrenal, ATN, AIN and: [AKI: postrenal (B/L hydronephroureteronephrosis on USG), pre-renal (normal urine analysis), ATN, AIN. (Book p749)]
Which statement about the AKI arm is TRUE? [Pre-renal investigation: normal urine analysis; postrenal: B/L hydronephroureteronephrosis (USG). (Book p749)]

Fill up: In the hours-to-days AKI list, ATN is expanded on this page as acute tubular ______. [The printed lines are 'Acute tubular nephrosis (ATN)' and 'Acute interstitial nephrosis (AIN)' — the page uses nephrosis for both, unlike the usual ne]

The postrenal line of the AKI branch reads B/L hydroureteronephrosis with USG written in brackets. [Printed: 'Postrenal : B/L hydroureteronephrosis (USG)'; the biopsy line belongs to RPGN in the days-to-weeks branch. (Book p749)]
Rapidly progressive renal failure most commonly turns out to be: [RPRF → RPGN (m/c), diagnosed with biopsy; severe ATN and TMA are rare causes. (Book p749)]

All of the following appear under rapidly progressive renal failure in the flowchart EXCEPT: [RPRF: RPGN (m/c), severe ATN, TMA; nephrotic syndrome sits under normal RFT with renal disease. (Book p749)]

Match each item of the hypertensive-crisis branch with its label — 1) Renal artery stenosis 2) Thrombotic microangiopathy 3) Hypertensive crisis … A) Small vessel kidney disease B) Large vessel kidney disease C) Vascular cause [Hypertensive crisis: vascular cause; RAS = large vessel kidney disease; TMA = small vessel kidney disease. (Book p749)]

Normal RFT with renal disease includes nephrotic syndrome, asymptomatic urine abnormality and: [Normal RFT with renal disease: nephrotic syn, renal tubular acidosis type I/II, asymptomatic urine abnormality. (Book p749)]
Renal artery stenosis is also known as: [AKA renovascular HTN (RVH) / renal artery occlusion disease (RAOD). (Book p749)]
Left untreated, renal artery stenosis can progress to: [Can progress to CKD / ischemic nephropathy. (Book p749)]
Which vessel-size statement is TRUE as per the flowchart? [RAS: large vessel kidney disease; TMA: small vessel kidney disease. (Book p749)]

In the days-to-weeks branch, the bracket 'Rare cause' is drawn against which two entries? [Under rapidly progressive renal failure the list is RPGN (m/c, diagnosed with biopsy), then severe ATN and TMA grouped by a bracket labelled 'Rare cau]

A 32-year-old has creatinine rising from 1.2 to 5.0 mg/dL in ten days with an active sediment and 2+ proteinuria. Following the non-CKD flowchart, the picture is: [The 'Days to weeks' arm carries rapidly progressive renal failure whose m/c cause is RPGN, diagnosed with biopsy; the tempo and the active sediment ex]

elements.source: Match each population with its most common cause of RAS — 1) Overall 2) Young population 3) Indian/Asian population … A) Takayasu arteritis B) Atherosclerosis C) Fibromuscular dysplasia [Overall: atherosclerosis; young population: fibromuscular dysplasia; Indian/Asian: Takayasu arteritis. (Book p750)]

In young males, the cause of RAS that involves the entire length of the renal artery with microaneurysms is: [Young males: polyarteritis nodosa – entire length renal artery – microaneurysm. (Book p750)]

Atherosclerotic RAS involves the proximal renal artery over 1-2 cm and becomes symptomatic beyond what occlusion? [Atherosclerosis: proximal renal artery (1-2 cm); symptomatic: >80% occlusion. (Book p750)]
Fill up: Fibromuscular dysplasia, the young-population cause, affects the ______ renal artery. [Fibromuscular dysplasia (arteriopathy): mid to distal renal artery. (Book p750)]
The female-to-male ratio written for Takayasu arteritis is: [Takayasu arteritis (F:M = 9:1), proximal renal artery. (Book p750)]
The types of RAS are explained by the Goldblatt: [Explain by Goldblatt: two kidney one clip model. (Book p750)]
The pathogenesis of unilateral RAS starts with the clue: [Unilateral RAS pathogenesis: asymmetric kidney size. (Book p750)]
The written vasoconstriction potency order is: [Vasoconstriction potency: urotension > endothelin > AT-II. (Book p750)]
The clinical feature and basic investigation picture of unilateral RAS are: [C/F: persistent HTN; basic investigation (RFT, urine analysis) normal range. (Book p750)]

In the affected kidney of unilateral RAS, the sequence after reduced RBF/perfusion is: [Affected kidney: ↓ RBF/perfusion → (+) renin angiotensin → (+) ↑ aldosterone → ↑ AT-II ↑↑ → profound vasoconstriction → ↑ BP → HTN/HTN crisis. (Book p]

Fill up: In the normal kidney, ↑ renal interstitial hydrostatic pressure reduces reabsorption from the ______, producing pressure natriuresis. [Normal kidney: ↑ RIHP → ↓ reabsorption from PCT → ↑ excretion of Na+/H2O (pressure natriuresis theory). (Book p750)]
Which statement about the normal (contralateral) kidney in unilateral RAS is TRUE? [Normal kidney: ↑ RBF/medullary flow → ↑ RIHP → ↓ PCT reabsorption → ↑ Na+/H2O excretion. (Book p750)]

The book's note lists asymmetric kidney in vesicoureteral reflux and renal artery stenosis; it is NOT listed for: [Asymmetric kidney seen in: vesicoureteral reflux; renal artery stenosis. (Book p750)]
In the affected kidney, the doubly-raised AT-II produces: [↑ Angiotensin II (AT-II) ↑↑ → profound vasoconstriction → ↑ blood pressure → HTN/HTN crisis. (Book p750)]

Of the four 'most common' branches, which two both name the proximal renal artery as the site? [Site lines: atherosclerosis — proximal renal artery (1–2 cm); Takayasu — proximal renal artery; fibromuscular dysplasia — mid to distal; polyarteritis]

Fill up: The page puts the word ______ in brackets after fibromuscular dysplasia, classifying it as a disease of the arterial wall. [The young-population branch reads 'Fibromuscular dysplasia (Arteriopathy) — mid to distal renal artery'. (Book p750)]

In the affected-kidney chain, the arrows carrying a '(+)' mark are the ones running into the renin–angiotensin system box and into the aldosterone box. [The printed chain is ↓RBF/perfusion →(+) renin angiotensin system →(+) ↑aldosterone → ↑angiotensin II (↑↑) → profound vasoconstriction → ↑BP → HTN/HTN]

A 26-year-old Indian woman with weak upper-limb pulses and severe hypertension is found to have a renal artery bruit. Which branch of the 'most common' tree fits her? [The Indian/Asian population branch is Takayasu arteritis with the F:m ratio printed as 9:1 and the proximal renal artery affected; FMD belongs to the ]
Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis becomes symptomatic once occlusion passes: [The overall branch reads 'Symptomatic: >80% occlusion' of the proximal 1–2 cm of the renal artery. (Book p750)]

The investigation of choice to confirm renal artery stenosis is: [IOC: CT renal angio or MR angiography (confirms the doppler screen). (Book p751)]
The drug of choice written for unilateral RAS is: [Treatment: ACE inhibitors / ARBs – (DOC). (Book p751)]
Percutaneous transluminal renal angioplasty (PTRA) is offered only if the kidney size is above: [PTRA – only if kidney size > 8 cm. (Book p751)]

The pair of CT/MR angiogram images drawn to the right of the renal doppler picture carries which caption? [The two panels (A and B, each with a white arrow) are captioned 'unilateral renal artery stenosis'; the separate caption 'Bilateral renal artery steno]

An 8 cm left kidney is normal and the right, stenosed kidney measures 6.5 cm; blood pressure is controlled on ramipril. Per the treatment block, angioplasty is: [The unilateral treatment block lists ACE inhibitors/ARBs (DOC) and PTRA '- Only if kidney size > 8 cm'; the 6.5 cm kidney fails that condition. (Book ]

The prognosis written for bilateral RAS is: [Bilateral RAS: poor prognosis. (Book p751)]

In bilateral RAS, loss of pressure natriuresis with ↓ RIHP leads to: [Loss of pressure natriuresis / ↓ RIHP → ↑ Na+/H2O retention → intravascular volume overload → recurrent flash pulmonary edema (d/t intravascular edema]
Which statement about the bilateral RAS diagram is TRUE? [The (−) arrow shows intravascular volume overload inhibiting the renin angiotensin system. (Book p751)]
Recurrent flash pulmonary edema in bilateral RAS is treated with: [Rx: B/L percutaneous transluminal renal angioplasty with stenting. (Book p751)]
For blood pressure control in bilateral RAS, the book lists diuretics as DOC while ACE inhibitors/ARBs are: [In BP: diuretics (DOC); ACE inhibitors / ARBs: C/I as they ↓ GFR. (Book p751)]

A smoker with bilateral RAS and an ejection fraction of 60% returns with two episodes of overnight breathlessness; CDU confirms bilateral stenosis. elements.source: The book's caution while interpreting flash pulmonary edema in this context is: [Note: every pulmonary edema is cardiac unless proven otherwise. (Book p752)]

The screening test named on this page is renal artery stenosis colour doppler ultrasound (CDU); its characteristic waveform clue is the: [Screening test: RAS colour doppler ultrasound (CDU); look for parvus tardus pattern. (Book p752)]
On CDU, a resistivity index (RI) at or above which value points to parenchymal disease (CKD)? [RI ≥ 0.8 → parenchymal disease: CKD. (Book p752)]
With RI < 0.8, the stenosis criteria that route the patient to CT/MR renal angiography are: [RI < 0.8 with PSV > 180 cm/s OR RAR > 3.5 OR ΔRI > 0.05 → CT/MR renal angiography (IOC). (Book p752)]
All of the following are CDU look-for criteria of RAS EXCEPT: [The book's velocity criterion is peak systolic velocity > 180 cm/s, not 80 cm/s. (Book p752)]

The IOC after a positive screen is CT/MR renal angiography; the gold standard that is both diagnostic and therapeutic is: [Conventional angiograph (gold standard): diagnostic and therapeutic. (Book p752)]
Which statement about fibromuscular dysplasia is TRUE? [Non atherosclerotic/non inflammatory arteriopathy; incident: m/c in young girls. (Book p752)]
The pathology of fibromuscular dysplasia is medial fibroplasia in the tunica media of the: [Involves middle to distal renal artery: medial fibroplasia in tunica media. (Book p752)]
Fibromuscular dysplasia is bilateral in the renal arteries in 25% of cases; the other 25% involve: [25% B/L renal artery, 25% involves cerebral vessels. (Book p752)]
The angiographic feature illustrated for medial fibromuscular dysplasia is the: [The "string of beads" feature in medial fibromuscular dysplasia. (Book p752)]
The treatment of choice for fibromuscular dysplasia, carrying a good prognosis, is: [Treatment: PTRA (good prognosis). (Book p752)]

The two round fluoroscopy images are headed 'Pre-op' and 'Post-op' and captioned 'Severe stenosis' and 'Good flow' respectively. [The heading row prints Pre-op over the first image and Post-op over the second, with the captions 'Severe stenosis' and 'Good flow' under them. (Book ]

Along with peak systolic velocity above 180 cm/s and RAR above 3.5, the colour doppler criteria accept a change in resistivity index greater than: [The RI < 0.8 arm reads: Peak systolic velocity > 180 cm/s OR RAR > 3.5 OR ΔRI > 0.05, all routing to CT/MR renal angiography. (Book p752)]

Fill up: When the colour doppler study is labelled 'Investigation inconclusive', the flowchart sends the patient for ______. [Both the RI ≥ 0.8 side path 'Investigation inconclusive' and the RI < 0.8 positive-criteria path converge on CT/MR renal angiography, marked (IOC). (B]

Fill up: Under 'Incident', fibromuscular dysplasia is stated to be most common in ______. [The FMD block reads: Non atherosclerotic/non inflammatory Arteriopathy; Incident: m/c in young girls; pathology — middle to distal renal artery, media]
